messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Data Scientist
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 40

**Patient Initials:** M.R.
**Age:** 25
**Occupation:** Data Scientist
**Therapist’s Notes – Session 4**

M.R. is a slender, neatly dressed young man who sits forward in the chair, his hands resting on his knees. He speaks with a careful, measured precision, as if he is presenting findings from a dataset. He describes his life before the trauma as “a clean model.” He was finishing his master’s in computational statistics, living with his girlfriend, Sofia, and their two-year-old son, Leo. He remembers the exact date—a Tuesday in late March—when Sofia called him from the pediatrician’s office, her voice a thin, frayed wire. “They found a mass. They’re sending us to the children’s hospital.”

M.R. tells me he did not panic. He ran a regression in his head. *Probability of a benign finding: high. Most pediatric abdominal masses are benign.* He drove to the hospital in a state of hyper-focused calm, mentally cataloging every exit, every traffic light. He remembers the smell of the pediatric oncology floor—a mix of antiseptic and stale apple juice. He remembers the doctor’s words, not as a sentence, but as a string of data points: *Stage 3 Wilms tumor. Aggressive. Chemotherapy. Surgery. Five-year survival rate: 85%.*

For M.R., 85% was not a comfort. It was a failure of margin. He began a silent, obsessive calculation. *What was the 15%? What were the variables?* He stopped sleeping. He stopped eating meals, subsisting on coffee and protein bars at his laptop. He built a spreadsheet. He logged every lab value, every scan result, every medication dose. He cross-referenced them with research papers from PubMed, building a survival model for his own son. He tells me, “If I could just find the pattern, I could fix it. I could optimize the outcome.”

Sofia handled the logistics—the hospital stays, the insurance calls, the meals. M.R. handled the data. He felt he was failing when he was not staring at a screen. He began to feel a physical revulsion toward the hospital waiting room. The sound of a child’s cry—any child’s cry—would make his stomach drop. He started wearing noise-canceling headphones even when he wasn’t listening to anything. He tells me, “I couldn’t let the noise in. The noise was chaos. The data was order.”

Leo is now four. He is in remission. His scans are clean. M.R. says this fact out loud, then immediately follows it with, “But the scan is only a snapshot. A single data point. It doesn’t tell you about the next time.”

He is back at work as a data scientist for a financial analytics firm. He describes his job as “perfect for me.” He builds predictive models for market trends. He is good at it. But lately, he finds himself unable to trust his own models. He will stare at a line of code, knowing it is correct, but his chest will tighten, and he will delete it and start over. He checks his work seven times before submitting it. His manager has noticed a drop in his output.

At home, he cannot sit still. He finds himself walking through the apartment at night, touching the corners of furniture, checking the locks. He has a new ritual: every night, he goes into Leo’s room and watches him breathe. He counts the breaths. He times them. If the rhythm is off—if one breath is shallower than the last—he cannot go back to bed. He will stand there for an hour, waiting for the pattern to normalize.

He and Sofia are distant. He knows this. He tells me, “She wants me to talk about it. But what is there to say? The data is in. We got lucky. The next time, we might not.” He avoids sex. He avoids physical touch. He feels a tightness in his chest when Leo climbs into his lap. He does not know if this is love or fear.

He rates his distress today at a 7 out of 10. He says he came because Sofia “scheduled it” and he “couldn’t find a valid counterargument.” He looks at his hands. He says, “I know I’m not okay. But I don’t know what okay looks like anymore. I only know how to calculate risk.”
